av_event.line_text: I'm on the shelves in a big supermarket. Replenishment, they call it, makes it sound posh. Mostly early mornings, so I'm stacking beans at five o'clock while everyone's asleep. It's alright, like, the lads are a laugh, but the half four alarm is killing me. I keep saying I'll do a course, personal training or plastering or something, and then I don't, do you know what I mean.
av_event.what: A middle-aged woman pushes the half-open bedroom door wider behind Rhys, leans in holding a mug, mouths something towards him, sets the mug down on the chest of drawers next to the TV and leaves, pulling the door back to half open. Rhys keeps talking without turning round.

text:
A: Hiya! Can you hear me alright? Sorry, I was miles away there.
B: Hello, yes, I can hear you. I'm Nasreen.
A: Rhys, nice one. How you doing, you alright?
B: Yeah, I'm okay, thank you. Bit tired, you know. You?
A: Knackered, mate, honest to God. I was up half four for work this morning, so that puzzle thing, my brain was not having it. Did you get them all?
B: Erm, not all. Some of them was hard. The one with the shapes.
A: The shapes! Yeah, I just sort of guessed that one, I'm not gonna lie.
B: Where are you from? Your accent is nice.
A: Aw, thanks. Caerphilly, South Wales. Got the castle, like. Rammed with tourists in summer. Where are you?
B: Walsall. West Midlands, near Birmingham.
A: Oh, tidy. I've been to Birmingham once for a gig. What do you do, then?
B: Erm, at the moment I'm between jobs, you know. Before, I was receptionist at a GP surgery.
A: Oh right, so you're the one on the phone at eight in the morning when everyone's ringing for an appointment?
B: Yes, that's right. Everybody shouting.
A: My mam goes mad at our surgery, honestly. She's on redial for like forty minutes.
B: Yeah, yeah. It's not the receptionist's fault, the system is like that. But I liked it. Talking to people, calming them down.
A: You seem like you'd be good at that, to be fair. Calming people down.
B: Thank you. What work you do?
A: I'm on the shelves in a big supermarket. Replenishment, they call it, makes it sound posh. Mostly early mornings, so I'm stacking beans at five o'clock while everyone's asleep. It's alright, like, the lads are a laugh, but the half four alarm is killing me. I keep saying I'll do a course, personal training or plastering or something, and then I don't, do you know what I mean.
B: You're young. You have time.
A: That's what my mam says. I'm still living at home with her and my dad, so I hear it every day, yeah?
B: My son is like you. Zain. He's seventeen. He eats everything in the fridge.
A: Ha! Sounds like me. Mam does the shop on a Saturday and it's gone by Tuesday.
B: Same. I buy yoghurts, next day, finished.
A: Is he at college?
B: Sixth form. He wants to do university. I hope.
A: Aw, fair play to him. Tell him to stick at it, honestly. I started a BTEC and packed it in, and I sort of wish I hadn't now.
B: You can go back.
A: Yeah. Yeah, maybe. Now in a minute, as we say.
B: Now in a minute?
A: Sorry, it's a Welsh thing. Means like, soon. Or never, depending who's saying it.
B: Acha. My partner is like that also. He says "I'll fix it", one year later, still not fixed.
A: Classic! Is he working today?
B: He drives taxi. Nights, mostly. So he's sleeping now.
A: Oh no, so we've got to keep it down, is it?
B: No, no, it's fine. He sleeps like—
